Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A black-capped chickadee perched on a curved autumn branch

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

17 stepsFocal point: the bird's head and black cap, upper middle Light: a low hazy sun at the upper right, so the right side of the bird, the top of the branch, and the right edges of the leaves catch the lightHow this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)
  • Ultramarine blue
  • Burnt sienna

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: Blend the misty sky from gray to goldFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: Paint the pale sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • old stiff 1/2 inch flat: Pull the far misty trunksOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • old stiff brush: Dab the dark hazy foliageOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • 1/2 inch angle: Pull the trunk and branch in dark barkAngle: flat cut on a slant, for crisp corners and curves
  • #10 round: Block in the four leavesRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #8 round: Light the sun side of the leaves in goldRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/2 inch filbert: Block in the body in warm apricotFilbert: flat with a rounded end, for soft-edged shapes
  • small fan brush: Flick in the pale chest feathersFan: bristles spread like a fan, for grass, fur, and soft blending
  • #4 round: Shade the dark wing stripesRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/4 inch flat: Light the pale feather edgesFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • liner: Line in the legs and feetLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • White canvas or canvas board
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

Before you start

Mark halves and quarters on tape

Run a strip of masking tape along the top edge of the canvas and one down a side, and mark the middle and the quarters on each. Every step's Where picture has the same lines, so you can find its place on your canvas. (Chalk lines on the canvas would be painted over by the first coat; the tape stays.)

The transfer outline (optional)

The outlines of the main shapes, on the same quarter grid as your tape: 1 The four leaves; 2 The chickadee. Before the stage that starts one, you can lightly chalk its outline on the canvas, using the tape marks to place it.

Strokes to try on scrap paper first

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

  • X stroke, first in step 1.
  • Small circles, first in step 2.
  • Dry brush, first in step 3. Try it on scrap paper first: wipe the brush until it leaves broken marks.
  • Dabbing, first in step 4.
  • Thick to thin, first in step 5.
  • Building from pieces, first in step 7.
  • Press and lift, first in step 8. Try a row of them on scrap paper first.
  • Curved strokes, first in step 10.
  • Flicking, first in step 11.
  • Liner work, first in step 17. Try a few lines on scrap paper first.

The basics

Before you start not checked yet

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.
Keep your colors clean not checked yet

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.
Colors dry darker not checked yet

Colors dry darker

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic looks lighter when wet than when dry.
  • Before a big area, paint a test swatch and let it dry before judging the mix.
Fixing a mistake not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.
Keep paint from drying on the palette not checked yet

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.
Let each layer dry not checked yet

Let each layer dry

Not checked yet

  • Between steps, the paint underneath should be dry to the touch. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  • Painting into half-dry paint drags it up and turns it gooey and muddy.
  • Thick paint can feel dry on top and still be wet inside. Give thick areas longer.
  • Fine lines and light colors over dark especially need a dry layer underneath.
Light colors over dark need more than one coat not checked yet

Light colors over dark need more than one coat

Not checked yet

  • One coat of white or a light color over a dark one usually looks gray and patchy.
  • Expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry. Use the paint thick, with little water.
Making a color lighter or darker not checked yet

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.
One light direction not checked yet

One light direction

Not checked yet

  • Pick where the light comes from and put every highlight on that side.
  • Each thing is built the same way: the whole shape in a darker or middle value, a lighter value on the side facing the light, then the lightest on a small area at the very edge. Each covers less than the one before.
The ugly stage not checked yet

The ugly stage

Not checked yet

  • Partway through, every painting looks flat or wrong. That's normal. Keep building.
  • Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.
  • Details come last, and only on shapes that are already right.
How much water not checked yet

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.

The misty sky 2 steps

STEP 1 OF 17 · The misty sky, 1 of 2

Blend the misty sky from gray to gold

  1. Inside the outlined area: the whole canvas.
  2. Paints, top to bottom: Sunset gold, then Misty blue-gray.
  3. Mix enough Sunset gold for this step and step 8; cover it between them.
  4. Mix enough Misty blue-gray for this step and steps 6, 14 and 16; cover it between them.
  5. Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: One or two colors on the brush. How much of each is on it controls the blend.
  6. Short strokes that cross each other in two directions, like overlapping X shapes.
  7. It should leave a soft, slightly textured blended fill with visible criss-cross marks.
  8. Watch out: Blending after the paint has started to drag. Acrylic sets in minutes, and scrubbing setting paint lifts it and leaves streaks. Fix: stop as soon as it drags.
  9. Let it dry, then blend a new thin layer on top.

Tip: The light comes from a low, hazy sun at the upper right, so every highlight in this painting goes on the right or top side. Start with the gold around the sun's spot, then work the gray in from the left and bottom edges, crossing strokes where they meet. Paint straight across the whole canvas, under where the branch and bird will go.

STEP 2 OF 17 · The misty sky, 2 of 2

Paint the pale sun

  1. Let the misty sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is a little below the top edge, and its right side is a little left of the 3/4 mark on the top tape.
  4. Paint: Pale sun yellow.
  5. Brush: #6 round.
  6. Small circles with the tip of the brush, moving outward from the middle of the sun, so its edge stays soft and glows into the gold.
  7. It should leave a bumpy, soft edge.
  8. Watch out: the edge is too hard. Fix: soften it with lighter circular passes.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The sun is a small circle, about the size of a coin on the canvas, in the middle of the brightest gold, as the Where picture shows. Keep its edge soft so it glows into the gold rather than sitting on it like a sticker.

The far woods 2 steps

STEP 3 OF 17 · The far woods, 1 of 2

Pull the far misty trunks

  1. Let the misty sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area, top to bottom to the right edge. Its left side is at the 3/4 mark on the top tape.
  4. Paint: Slate gray.
  5. Mix enough Slate gray for this step and steps 12 and 17; cover it between them.
  6. Brush: old stiff 1/2 inch flat. Load: A dry brush, no water. Load only the tip, then wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel. It should feel dry and hard to apply.
  7. Light pressure, skimming the surface.
  8. It should leave feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.
  9. Watch out: trunks that look like stiff, even posts. Fix: let the width wobble a little and keep the edges broken and soft.

Tip: There are two main trunks, straight up and down, with a fainter one between and left of them. Pull each stroke from the top edge down to the bottom. Keep them broken and soft so the mist and gold show through: they're far away, so no light side and no bark.

STEP 4 OF 17 · The far woods, 2 of 2

Dab the dark hazy foliage

  1. Let the far misty trunks and the misty sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  3. Paint: Warm apricot.
  4. Mix enough Warm apricot for this step and step 9; cover it between them.
  5. Brush: old stiff brush. Load: Little paint, fairly dry.
  6. Tap with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.
  7. It should leave dots or dappled patches that get more solid the more you tap.
  8. Watch out: Blobs instead of dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Fix: wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Dab loose clumps, most of them on the right half around the trunks and along the left edge, with a few low in the bottom middle. Leave plenty of the gray mist showing between the clumps. Keep them blurry: they're far behind the bird.

The branch 2 steps

STEP 5 OF 17 · The branch, 1 of 2

Pull the trunk and branch in dark bark

  1. Let the far woods and the misty sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, top to bottom from the left edge. Its right side is at the right edge.
  3. Paint: Dark bark brown.
  4. Mix enough Dark bark brown for this step and step 17; cover it between them.
  5. Brush: 1/2 inch angle.
  6. Press the full width of the brush for the thick part, then turn onto its edge or tip and lighten the pressure. With an angle brush, the lighter you press, the thinner the line.
  7. It should leave a line that starts wide and tapers to a point: wide at the trunk, thin at the twig tips.
  8. Watch out: Branches that look like stiff sticks. Every branch the same width and straight. Fix: start thick at the trunk and taper. Let branches fork in different directions and overlap.

Tip: The trunk rises up the left side and the branch curves out from its lower part in one long arch, highest under the bird, then dipping to the lower right. Pull each stroke along the branch, wide at the trunk end and thinner toward the twig tips. Add the two thin twigs at the right end and the leaf stems last, with the tip of the brush.

STEP 6 OF 17 · The branch, 2 of 2

Dry-brush the light onto the bark

  1. Let the branch and the far woods dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, top to bottom from the left edge. Its right side is at the right edge.
  3. Paints, darkest first: Warm bark brown, then Misty blue-gray. The paint map shows where each goes.
  4. Brush: old stiff 1/2 inch flat. Load: A dry brush, no water. Load only the tip, then wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel. It should feel dry and hard to apply.
  5. Light pressure, skimming the surface.
  6. It should leave feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.
  7. Leave what step 5 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Misty blue-gray is much lighter than what it goes over: expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry.
  9. Watch out: It went on solid. The brush was too loaded. Fix: let it dry, then dry-brush the base color back over part of it.
  10. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Drag the brush along the length of the branch, never across it, with the warm brown over most of the top half and the cool gray in a few short drags right on the top edge, facing the sun. Keep the dark brown showing along the bottom edge of the branch and the left side of the trunk, the side away from the sun.

The four leaves 2 steps

STEP 7 OF 17 · The four leaves, 1 of 2

Block in the four leaves

  1. Let the branch and the far woods dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, placed with the tape marks.
  3. Inside the outlined area, top to bottom. Its left side is a little left of the 1/4 mark on the top tape and its right side is a little left of the right edge.
  4. Paints, darkest first: Leaf red-orange, then Leaf orange. The paint map shows where each goes.
  5. Brush: #10 round.
  6. Start each leaf with one simple pointed oval. Then add the lobes in small curved pieces on each side, smaller toward the tip.
  7. It should leave four leaf shapes made of distinct pieces, with small gaps or overlaps between them.

Tip: There are four leaves: a yellow one at the top edge, a red one hanging below it beside the trunk, and a yellow and a red one hanging under the right side of the branch. Lay the orange where the yellow leaves go and the red-orange for the two red ones, as the paint map shows. Each leaf is a pointed shape with a few jagged lobes, its point hanging down.

STEP 8 OF 17 · The four leaves, 2 of 2

Light the sun side of the leaves in gold

  1. Let the four leaves and the branch dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, top to bottom. Its left side is a little left of the 1/4 mark on the top tape and its right side is at the 3/4 mark on the top tape.
  3. Paint: Sunset gold.
  4. Brush: #8 round. Load: Paint loaded well into the belly of the brush, creamy, not runny.
  5. Touch down with the tip, press so the belly spreads, then pull and lift so the stroke ends on the tip.
  6. It should leave a teardrop or comma shape, wide where you pressed and pointed where you lifted.
  7. Leave what step 7 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Watch out: A blob instead of a teardrop. Too much paint, or too slow a lift. Fix: use less paint and lift faster.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Press the gold onto the two yellow leaves, more on their right sides toward the sun, and add a touch along the right edge of the red ones. Leave a thin line of orange down the middle of each yellow leaf: that's its vein.

Press and lift also called comma stroke, petal stroke, leaf stroke

Not checked yet

With. round

Load. Paint loaded well into the belly of the brush, creamy, not runny.

Motion. Touch down with the tip, press so the belly spreads, then pull and lift so the stroke ends on the tip.

What it leaves. A teardrop or comma shape, wide where you pressed and pointed where you lifted.

Then. Tidy the edges with the background color once dry.

Press, pull, lift

If it goes wrong.

  • A blob instead of a teardrop. Too much paint, or too slow a lift. Use less paint and lift faster.

The chickadee's body 3 steps

STEP 9 OF 17 · The chickadee's body, 1 of 3

Block in the body in warm apricot

STEP 11 OF 17 · The chickadee's body, 3 of 3

Flick in the pale chest feathers

  1. Let the chickadee and the far woods dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is a little above the 1/4 mark on the side tape, and its left side is at the 1/4 mark on the top tape.
  3. Paint: Pale buff.
  4. Brush: small fan brush. Load: Light paint. Too much makes flat blobs.
  5. A quick stroke from inside the chest, lifting off in the direction the feathers lie, down and back from the head, so each mark thins at its end.
  6. It should leave short tapered feather marks with broken tips.
  7. Leave what steps 9 and 10 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Watch out: The feathers turn into a flat smooth patch. Too much paint on the brush, or the strokes are blended together.
  9. Fix: wipe the brush nearly dry, make each flick short and separate, and let it dry before adding more.
  10. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The chest just under the black bib, on the right side facing the sun, gets the most and the palest flicks. Fewer go lower down and toward the wing. Leave the apricot showing between flicks, and the tan under the belly.

Light the pale feather edges

The feet 1 step

STEP 17 OF 17 · The feet, 1 of 1

Line in the legs and feet

  1. Let the chickadee's body and the branch dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is a little above the 3/4 mark on the side tape, and its left side is a little left of the middle mark on the top tape.
  4. Paints, darkest first: Soft black, Dark bark brown, then Slate gray. The paint map shows where each goes.
  5. Brush: liner. Load: Thin the paint with water until it flows like ink: swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Reload often.
  6. Hold the brush upright, with light, steady pressure. Pull each leg down from the belly, then the toes curling over the branch, and wobble the edges a little.
  7. It should leave thin, flowing lines.
  8. Watch out: Lines that feather or spread. Laid into a wet layer underneath. Fix: let the area underneath dry first.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: There are two legs, a short way apart, each angled down from the belly to the top of the branch. The toes curl over the front of the branch, dark with a touch of gray on their tops. Touch the dark bark brown back in between the toes where the legs crossed it. This is the last step: the painting is finished when they're on.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A black-capped chickadee perched on a curved brown branch with a few orange and yellow leaves, in front of a hazy blue-gray and orange autumn forest with a pale sun at the upper right.

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: No bars, borders, captions, watermarks, or surrounding scene; the whole image is the painting.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: No tiny separate things (no houses, people, fences). The background foliage is already loose soft dabs, not single leaves; the tree trunks in the haze are a few soft vertical bands; the only crisp leaves are four big ones. The parts (haze sky, sun glow, far trunks, far foliage dabs, branch, leaves, bird) fit the budget of 8.

Why: Every texture is already one repeated loose mark a beginner can make, so a beginner version would change nothing worth its render.

A small bird is the whole point: the chickadee's black cap and white cheek against a glowing, misty autumn wood. The background is soft and loose and should stay that way; the hard parts for a beginner are the bird's shape, its feathered chest, and the long arching branch.

Subject: A black-capped chickadee perched on a curved autumn branch
Focal point: the bird's head and black cap, upper middle
Light: a low hazy sun at the upper right, so the right side of the bird, the top of the branch, and the right edges of the leaves catch the light

What it saw, back to front

  1. Misty sunset sky
  2. The branch
  3. The four leaves
  4. The chickadee
  5. Legs and feet
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Paint-along, back to front, fits a soft misty background with a branch and a bird in front, at beginner level, and it's the only technique with version 2 keys.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner.yaml)

No version 2 keys, and the owner's pick for beginner acrylic is paint-along.

How the paint recipes were worked out13 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

  • Misty blue-gray Delta E 3.1
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts white, 1 part ultramarine, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of yellow

  • Sunset gold Delta E 1.6
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 4 parts white, 2 parts yellow, 2 parts burnt sienna, 1 part red

  • Pale sun yellow Delta E 0.6
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 12 parts white, 3 parts yellow, 1 part red

  • Slate gray Delta E 3.9
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts white, 2 parts ultramarine, 2 parts burnt sienna, a touch of yellow

  • Warm apricot Delta E 3.1
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts red, 2 parts white, 1 part yellow, 1 part ultramarine

  • Dark bark brown Delta E 3.1
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts ultramarine, 3 parts burnt sienna, 2 parts red

  • Warm bark brown Delta E 1.5
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts burnt sienna, 1 part red, 1 part ultramarine, 1 part white

  • Leaf red-orange Delta E 0.8
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts red, 2 parts burnt sienna, 1 part white, a touch of ultramarine

  • Leaf orange Delta E 2.2
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts yellow, 2 parts red, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of white

  • Pale buff Delta E 0.5
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 4 parts white, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of yellow

  • Shadow tan Delta E 2.8
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts burnt sienna, 2 parts white, a touch of ultramarine

  • Soft black Delta E 4.4
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 1 part ultramarine, 1 part burnt sienna

  • Warm white Delta E 1.6
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 6 parts white, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of yellow

Furthest off: Delta E 4.4. Real tubes vary by brand, so mix, compare with the step picture, and nudge.

Why the steps go in this order17 steps

Back to front: the misty sky blended wet first, the sun on it, the far trunks and foliage dabs, then the branch, the leaves hanging from it, the bird's body, its wing, cap, and cheek on top, and the legs last because they cross over the branch.

  1. 1. Blend the misty sky from gray to gold

    The whole canvas is mist and glow, so it's blended wet first and run straight under everything.

  2. 2. Paint the pale sun

    A small pale accent that sits on the gold glow, painted once the sky is dry.

  3. 3. Pull the far misty trunks

    The farthest solid things, soft gray verticals, before the foliage that overlaps them.

  4. 4. Dab the dark hazy foliage

    Far leaf masses dabbed over the mist and trunks, still behind the branch.

  5. 5. Pull the trunk and branch in dark bark

    The branch and trunk's dark first, as one flowing shape, before anything that hangs from or sits on it.

  6. 6. Dry-brush the light onto the bark

    The bark's warm middle and cool lit top, dry-brushed along the branch once the dark is dry.

  7. 7. Block in the four leaves

    The four leaves hang from the branch, so they go on after it, in their base reds and oranges.

  8. 8. Light the sun side of the leaves in gold

    Gold on the sun side of the leaves, over the dry base.

  9. 9. Block in the body in warm apricot

    The whole bird as one apricot shape first, cap and wing included, so later parts sit on it.

  10. 10. Shade the belly in tan

    The small shadow under the belly, the dark value of the body.

  11. 11. Flick in the pale chest feathers

    The pale chest feathers flicked over the dry body, the light value and the texture.

  12. 12. Block in the wing and tail in slate gray

    The gray wing and tail over the body.

  13. 13. Shade the dark wing stripes

    Dark stripes on the dry wing.

  14. 14. Light the pale feather edges

    Pale edges on the wing and tail, last of the wing's values.

  15. 15. Paint the black cap and bib

    The black cap and bib, the focal point, on top of the body.

  16. 16. Paint the white cheek

    The white cheek between the cap and bib, once the black is dry.

  17. 17. Line in the legs and feet

    The legs cross over the branch, so they're last, and they finish the painting.

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • Feathers: no library element fit the chickadee's body (short feather strokes over a block-in). Drafted feathered-body in elements/ and filed it as https://github.com/DeanPhillipsOKC/gesso/issues/112. The research has no section on feathers or birds; the flicking card (grass and fur) was the closest stroke.
  • Rewrote card lines for this subject: curved-strokes (pumpkin ribs) on the belly, wing stripes, and cheek; small-circles (clouds) on the sun; flicking (upward grass) for feathers lying down and back; build-from-pieces (( ) pieces) on leaves, the bird, the wing, and the cap; liner (branches) on the legs; thick-to-thin result (branches and grass) on the branch; and the trunks-branches element mistake (forking branches) on the far trunks.
  • The branch's first outline (width 0.07) took warm foliage dabs and the area under the bird as bark, which made big leaf-shaped blobs in the dark bark step. A narrower width plus points_out on those dabs fixed it, but cost the branch's thick underside until a path along it was added.
  • paints --add found no second color for the foliage or a third for the branch, so the far foliage is one paint and the bark's light top rides in the warm brown pass. The cool gray light pass on the bark changed only specks and was folded into the brown pass.
  • The bird's beak and eye are too small to outline; they ride on the cap step without a paint of their own.
  • There was no Agent tool in this run, so the text review was done in the same context (review_context: same).

Known problems

Where the pictures aren't quite right. Paint it the way the step says and use the picture as a guide.

  • Step 1, Blend the misty sky from gray to gold: The blend picture shows faint shapes of the foliage and a dark stub at the right, and a brown sliver of the trunk at the bottom-left corner, in what's painted as one smooth blend.
  • Step 4, Dab the dark hazy foliage: The far foliage ranges from red-orange to gold, but the step has one paint, Warm apricot.
  • Step 15, Paint the black cap and bib: The gray beak and the eye's tiny light show in this step, but its only paint is Soft black.
  • The text review was done by the same session that wrote the text, not a fresh one.
